extracted.intended_audience: writers, humorists, comedians, copywriters, public speakers, and storytellers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on applying the 'rule of three' across writing, comedy, advertising, rhetoric, storytelling and visual composition: when and how to use triads for memorability, humour, and rhetorical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of three (core principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: A writing principle which suggests that a trio of entities such as examples, events, or characters is more satisfying, effective, or humorous than other numbers, hence also more memorable, because it combines both brevity and rhythm with the smallest amount of information needed to create a pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use groups of three (words, phrases, sentences, events, characters, sections, or whole books) to create a memorable, rhythmic pattern that balances brevity with enough information to establish and exploit a pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tricolon (equal-form triad)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tricolon is a more specific use of the rule of three where three words or phrases are equal in length and grammatical form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for formal rhetorical balance or emphasis, construct three parallel elements equal in grammatical form and (ideally) length to increase cadence and perceived strength of the statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hendiatris (single idea via three words)
rubrics_metrics.description: A hendiatris is a figure of speech where three successive words are used to express a single central idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use three short successive words to distill and emphasize a single concept (e.g., 'life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness'); this can make mottos and slogans punchy and memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tripartite motto / slogan structure
rubrics_metrics.description: As a slogan or motto, grouping concepts into three parts (a tripartite motto) creates a catchy, memorable formulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For public messages and branding, prefer three-part slogans to aid recall and rhythmic delivery; examples include national mottos and widely recognized safety slogans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising copywriting triad (E. St. Elmo Lewis: attract–interest–convince)
rubrics_metrics.description: E. St. Elmo Lewis's three chief copywriting principles: attract a reader so they will look at the advertisement and start to read it; interest them so they will continue; then convince them so they will believe it. If an advertisement contains these three qualities of success, it is a successful advertisement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure ad copy to sequentially (1) attract attention, (2) maintain interest, and (3) convince/convert; ensure all three functions are present for effective advertising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy: set up two, subvert with the third (comic triple)
rubrics_metrics.description: In comedy the third element of the triple is often used to create an effect of surprise with the audience and is frequently the punch line of the joke itself. The comedic rule of threes relies on setting up a pattern of two items and then subverting viewer expectations by breaking that pattern with the third item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build a pattern with the first two items, then break or twist that pattern on the third to create surprise and humour; the third element typically contains the punch line or unexpected turn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy: timing and tension/release
rubrics_metrics.description: The comedic rule of three is often paired with quick timing, ensuring that viewers have less time to catch on to the pattern before the punch line hits. Just like most comedic writing, the rule of threes in comedy relies on building tension to a comedic release: tension is built with the first two items and then released with the final item, which should be the funniest of the three.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver the triple with tight pacing so the audience has minimal time to anticipate the twist; make the third element the funniest and the one that releases built tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triple length guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Most triples are short in length, often only two or three sentences, but the rule can also be implemented effectively at longer length as long as base formula is still followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer compact triples for immediacy, but longer examples are acceptable if they maintain the setup–subversion–punch structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual-art use of three to imply 'some'
rubrics_metrics.description: In visual arts, three elements are used to convey 'some' (e.g., three rocks imply 'some rocks'); two would read as a pair and four may be 'one more than necessary.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing backgrounds or scenes, use three repeated elements to imply plurality without clutter; three is the minimal number that reads as 'some' rather than a pair or an overabundance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storytelling/folklore triplets and three-part structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Storytellers often create triplets or structures in three parts—simplest form: beginning, middle, and end. Folk tales commonly repeat or negate elements twice so they occur thrice (e.g., three tests, three visits, youngest son is the third).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use triadic repetition in plot beats, tasks, or visits to build expectation and payoff; threefold trials or gifts are a conventional folktale device that signals pattern and resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric/public speaking: use tripling for emphasis and applause
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of a series of three elements is a well-known feature of public oratory to generate what some call 'claptraps'—three-part phrases in speeches often evoke audience applause and increase rhetorical impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ three-part lists or phrases in speeches to increase memorability and to rhythmically cue the audience for rhetorical peaks (e.g., 'justice, good will, and brotherhood').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding overuse (LLM and AI writing anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Large language models often use the rule of three. AI writing may overuse the rule of three, especially when using adjectives, leading to writing which feels verbose but lacking in depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful not to default to triads mechanically—overuse can make text feel repetitive or shallow; vary structure and use triads intentionally for effect rather than habit.
